title: Continuity Detective
description: Read original, invented scene notes to spot the mismatched detail, match each slip to the crew role that would catch it, then put takes in an order that keeps the scene consistent.

sections.title: Spot the slip
sections.description: Find the detail that breaks continuity.

sections.title: Who catches it?
sections.description: Match the problem to a crew role.

sections.title: Order the takes
sections.description: Sequence shots so details stay consistent.

questions.prompt: Which detail in this scene note breaks continuity?
questions.context: Invented scene note: Mia pours coffee into a mug until it is full. In a later shot of the same unbroken moment, she lifts the mug without drinking, and it is empty. Rain taps the window throughout.

options.label: Mia pours coffee into the mug
The mug goes from full to empty with no drinking

questions.explanation: Contents of a prop must change only through shown action. Nothing explains the missing coffee, so the viewer notices a mismatch between shots.

questions.prompt: Which detail in this invented note fails to match between shots?
questions.context: Invented scene note: In the wide shot, Dev enters with a zipped jacket and a red umbrella in his left hand. He never sets it down or passes it over. In the close-up, the umbrella is in his right hand.

options.label: Dev's jacket is zipped in both shots
Dev enters during the wide shot
The umbrella switches hands with no action shown

questions.explanation: Hand placement is a classic continuity detail. Without a shown handoff, the umbrella jumping between hands looks like an error when the shots are cut together.

questions.prompt: In this invented kitchen scene, which detail cannot be consistent?
questions.context: Invented scene note: One continuous 90-second kitchen scene begins with a wall clock at 6:00 and a candle 10 cm tall, burning. At the end, the clock reads 6:01 and the candle is 14 cm tall. The window shows dusk throughout.

options.label: A burning candle ending taller than it began
The scene being set in a kitchen

questions.explanation: A burning candle gets shorter, not taller. Ninety seconds fits a clock moving from 6:00 to 6:01, so the clock is fine.

questions.prompt: Which role on this invented crew sheet should have caught the cardigan mismatch?
questions.context: Invented crew sheet. Costume supervisor: tracks what each character wears in every take. Sound mixer: records dialogue and room tone. Gaffer: leads the lighting crew. Location manager: arranges access to filming sites. Case: Mia's cardigan is buttoned in one take and open in the next, in the same moment.
questions.explanation: Wardrobe state across takes is the costume supervisor's job in this sheet. The other roles cover audio, lighting and filming-site access.

questions.prompt: Which role on this invented sheet should have caught the door-and-line mismatch?
questions.context: Invented crew sheet. Script supervisor: logs the order of action, dialogue and timing in each take. Gaffer: leads the lighting crew. Location manager: arranges access to filming sites. Sound mixer: records dialogue and room tone. Case: In take 1 Ana says "Ready" and then closes the door. In take 2 she closes the door first.
questions.explanation: The order of action versus dialogue is exactly what this sheet assigns to the script supervisor. Without matching order, the two takes cannot be cut together smoothly.

questions.prompt: Order these takes so Mia's coffee stays consistent from start to finish.
questions.context: Invented rules: a mug must be filled before it is lifted. She lifts it before sipping. The empty mug is shown only after she has sipped.

items.label: Mia pours coffee into the mug
Close-up of the empty mug on the table

questions.explanation: Each rule links neighbours in a single chain: pour, lift, sip, then the empty mug. Reversing any pair would make the coffee level look wrong.

questions.prompt: Order these takes so Dev's umbrella stays consistent. Which can go anywhere?
questions.context: Invented rules: the umbrella is closed only after it was opened outside. Drips on the shop mat are shown only after it is closed. Dev hanging his coat has no link to the umbrella.

items.label: Dev closes the umbrella at the shop door
Drips appear on the shop mat
Dev hangs his coat on a hook

questions.explanation: The umbrella chain is open, close, drips. The coat action is independent in these rules, so it can sit anywhere without breaking continuity.

questions.prompt: Order the shots in the edited scene so both continuity chains hold.
questions.context: Invented screen-story rules: sunlight appears on the wall before it appears on the floor. The lamp glow appears only after sunlight reaches the floor. Ana's sleeve appears wet only after the splash shot.

items.label: Wide shot with sunlight on the wall
Medium shot with sunlight on the floor
Take where water splashes Ana's sleeve

questions.explanation: There are two independent chains: the light sequence and the sleeve sequence. Editing arranges shots into a scene, so the edited order must keep each chain intact, while takes from the two chains can interleave freely.

title: Film Craft Decoder
description: Match film terms to plain definitions, then decode original text-only scene descriptions and contrast similar camera and editing techniques.

questions.prompt: Match each film term to its plain-language definition.
questions.explanation: Editing arranges shots and scenes and joins image with sound; an extreme close-up isolates a tiny detail; tracking moves the camera; a zoom changes the lens.

right.label: Arranging shots and scenes and combining image with sound
Framing that isolates one very small detail
The camera itself changes position while filming
The lens changes the framing; the camera can stay put

questions.prompt: A camera sits on a wheeled cart and rolls beside a runner along a whole street. Which term fits?
questions.explanation: The camera physically changes position to follow the runner, which is what a tracking shot is.
questions.context: These scenes are original text descriptions written for this quiz, not film clips.

questions.prompt: A single key turning in a lock fills the whole screen, and nothing else is visible. Which term fits?
questions.explanation: Framing that isolates one tiny detail, here the key, is an extreme close-up.

questions.prompt: Shots alternate: a chef plating dessert, a courier cycling toward the restaurant, chef, courier, as both happen at once. Which term fits?
questions.explanation: Alternating between scenes that happen at the same time is cross-cutting, an editing structure, as defined in this quiz's supplied term list.
questions.context: Supplied term: cross-cutting means editing that alternates between two or more scenes taking place at the same time.

questions.prompt: A camera stays fixed on a tripod while the lens gradually tightens from a wide view of a market to one vendor's face. What happened?
questions.explanation: The camera did not move; only the lens changed the framing, which describes a zoom rather than a tracking shot.

options.label: An extreme close-up of a small object

questions.prompt: For each described action, decide whether it is a tracking shot or a zoom.
questions.explanation: If the camera's position changes, it is tracking. If only the lens changes the framing from a fixed spot, it is a zoom.

cells.label: Camera glides on rails toward an actor
Camera locked on a stand; lens magnifies a distant sign
Operator walks backward carrying the camera ahead of a dancer

questions.prompt: Which description is an extreme close-up rather than an ordinary close-up?
questions.explanation: An extreme close-up isolates a small detail, such as an eyelid; head-and-shoulders or wider framings include much more.

options.label: Head and shoulders of a singer fill the frame
Only an eyelid and lashes fill the frame
A full-length figure stands in a doorway
A whole room is visible from a corner

questions.prompt: Which change was made in editing rather than by moving or adjusting the camera?
questions.explanation: Editing arranges shots, so joining a kitchen shot to a street shot is an editing choice; the other options describe camera or lens actions.

options.label: The camera rolls forward on a cart
A kitchen shot is joined directly to a street shot
The lens is twisted to enlarge the view
The operator walks alongside the actor

title: Adaptation Switchboard
description: Solve original, invented adaptation briefs by linking proposed edits to production constraints, checking combined edits, and ordering a revision pass.

sections.title: Constraints to Edits
sections.description: Link single edits to the rules they satisfy.

sections.title: Combining Edits
sections.description: Test groups of edits against the full brief.

questions.prompt: Link each edit to every constraint its stated effect satisfies. Some constraints may be served by more than one edit, and some edits by more than one constraint.
questions.context: Invented brief: a short film called The Lantern Keeper, adapted from a long novel. Constraints: one lighthouse location, ten minutes, three speaking roles at most, daylight shooting only, no animals on set.

left.label: Play the market scene as a radio call taken inside the lighthouse
Compress the story into one afternoon, so it runs ten minutes with no night shots
Merge the ferryman and harbor master into one visitor, leaving three speaking roles
Replace the lighthouse dog with a bark added in editing
Delete the midnight storm scene, which required night filming

questions.explanation: Only the afternoon compression addresses two rules, runtime and daylight. The storm cut also serves daylight, so that constraint is shared by two edits.

questions.prompt: Which cut list brings the draft to ten minutes or less while keeping both required scenes?
questions.context: Invented draft: one script page equals one minute. Scenes: A is 6 pages, B is 5, C is 4, D is 5, E is 4. The draft totals 24 pages. Scenes C and E must stay.
questions.explanation: Cutting A, B and D removes 16 pages, leaving C and E at 8 minutes. The other lists either run too long or remove a required scene.

questions.prompt: Link each series constraint to every proposed edit whose stated effect satisfies it.
questions.context: Invented brief: a six-episode series adapted from a puzzle game called Tidefall. Constraints: keep the hero wordless, make each episode friendly to newcomers, and use only two interior sets per episode.

left.label: Keep the hero free of voiceover
Only two interior sets per episode

right.label: Open with a ten-second picture card explaining the game's rules
Show her thoughts as notebook sketches instead of voiceover
Limit interiors to the ferry and the café in every episode
Give each episode a visitor whose problem is introduced and solved within it

questions.explanation: Two edits serve the newcomer rule, since both make an episode understandable alone. The notebook and the two-interior limit each answer exactly one constraint.

questions.prompt: Which edit respects both the single-kitchen location and the two-on-screen-actors limit?
questions.context: Invented brief: a stage play becomes a short film shot entirely inside one kitchen, with at most two actors on screen. The story needs a cook, a neighbor and an inspector.

options.label: Cut away to the neighbor's garden for the argument
Seat the cook, neighbor and inspector together at the table
Show the cook and neighbor on screen; the inspector is a knock and a letter slid under the door
Add a market flashback with the cook and her brother

questions.explanation: The knock and letter keep the inspector present in the story without adding a third actor or leaving the kitchen. The other options add a location or too many actors.

questions.prompt: Match each edit to the production pressure it relieves. Several edits can relieve the same pressure.
questions.context: Invented novel-to-film brief about a farmhouse story. Each edit's effect is given in its label.

left.label: Merge the twin aunts into one character
Shoot the train-platform goodbye on the farmhouse porch
Remove a scene where the heroine explains the map a second time
Combine the postman and sheriff into one visitor
Reuse one hallway for three school-corridor scenes

questions.explanation: Merging characters shrinks the cast, relocating or reusing sets cuts locations, and deleting a repeated explanation shortens runtime. Cast and location each have two edits.

questions.prompt: Which pair of edits makes the draft meet all three limits of the brief?
questions.context: Invented draft: 16 minutes, 3 locations, 4 actors. Limits: 12 minutes, 2 locations, 3 actors. Edit 1: minus 2 minutes, minus 1 location. Edit 2: minus 1 minute, minus 1 actor. Edit 3: minus 3 minutes. Edit 4: minus 2 minutes, minus 1 actor.
questions.explanation: Only Edit 1 removes a location. Pairing it with Edit 4 gives 12 minutes, 2 locations and 3 actors. Edits 1 and 2 leave 13 minutes.

questions.prompt: For each combination of edits, decide whether the draft would meet every limit in the brief.
questions.context: Invented animated short The Paper Kite. Draft: 10 minutes, 4 backgrounds, 3 characters. Limits: 8 minutes, 2 backgrounds, 2 characters. Edit P: minus 2 minutes, minus 2 backgrounds. Edit Q: minus 1 character, minus 1 minute. Edit R: minus 1 background, minus 3 minutes.

cells.label: P and Q together
P and R together
Q and R together
P, Q and R together

questions.explanation: P and Q reach 7 minutes, 2 backgrounds, 2 characters. P and R leave 3 characters, and Q and R leave 3 backgrounds. All three edits meet every limit.

questions.prompt: Put this revision pass in a workable order, honoring the dependencies described.
questions.context: Invented revision workflow. You cannot mark scenes before the limits are written down. Relocation needs the marked list. Counting roles and timing a table read both need the relocated draft, but not each other.

items.label: Mark scenes outside the single location
Relocate marked scenes into the location
Count speaking roles in the relocated draft
Time a table read of the relocated draft

questions.explanation: The first three steps form a chain. Counting roles and timing the read are independent of each other, so either order after relocation is valid.

title: Cozy or Creepy Scene Lab
description: Answer four film-craft questions on shots, editing and lighting terms, then choose which atmosphere recipes you would rather linger in. Craft accuracy and atmosphere taste are shown separately.

sections.title: Craft Terms
sections.description: Four questions with right answers.

sections.title: Atmosphere Taste
sections.description: Four picks with no right answers.

dimensions.description: Whether you lean toward comforting or uneasy atmospheres when you choose a scene to linger in.
Whether lighting and image or sound and silence does more of the mood work for you.

questions.prompt: A still camera frames only a fingertip on a door latch, filling the whole screen. Which shot is this?
questions.explanation: An extreme close-up isolates a small detail, so a fingertip filling the frame is a classic example. The camera stays put and nothing needs to cut or move.

questions.prompt: The camera physically glides forward along a hallway on a dolly while the lens setting never changes. What is that called?
questions.explanation: A tracking camera changes its position through space. A lens zoom does not need the camera to move at all, which is the key difference.

questions.context: Working definitions. Practical light: a lamp or bulb visible in the scene that really lights it. Room tone: the faint background sound of a space. Long take: one shot held for a long time without cutting. Low-key lighting: mostly shadow with only a few small bright areas.
questions.prompt: Match each example to the technique it demonstrates.
questions.explanation: Each example shows one defined technique: a visible lamp is practical light, quiet air is room tone, an uncut shot is a long take, and a mostly dark frame is low-key.

left.label: A lamp stands in frame, throwing amber glow across a table
A faint recorded hum of an empty room under a silent scene
One unbroken shot lasting forty seconds
A face half hidden, most of the frame dark with one small bright source

questions.prompt: An editor joins three shots of an empty street and lays soft rain sound beneath them. What is editing doing here?
questions.explanation: Editing arranges shots and scenes and combines image with sound. It does not move the camera or change the lens, which happen during shooting.

options.label: Moving the camera through the street
Zooming the lens toward a detail
Isolating one small detail in frame
Arranging shots and combining image with sound

questions.prompt: Which scene recipe would you most like to linger in?
questions.explanation: No right answer here. Each recipe leans cozy or creepy, and relies more on lighting or on sound.

options.label: A quiet kitchen with a warm lamp glow and a steady, unhurried frame
A dim room with rain on the window and a kettle murmuring
An empty hallway under flickering fluorescent tubes, nothing audible
A black screen with humming lights and one distant footstep

questions.prompt: Rank these ingredients from the one you most want in a scene to the one you want least.
questions.explanation: This is a taste ranking, not a test. Your order shows which ingredients you enjoy most.

items.label: Deep shadow down an empty corridor

questions.prompt: When a scene sets its mood, how much do you feel lighting versus sound is doing the work?
questions.explanation: Neither end is correct. This shows whether you notice mood through what you see or what you hear.

questions.prompt: For each setting, pick the treatment you would most enjoy watching.
questions.explanation: These are personal picks with no correct pairing. Several settings can share the same treatment.

right.label: Slow camera drift with amber light
Gentle room tone and murmuring voices
Humming silence broken by one small noise

title: The Unreliable Narrator Files
description: Read eight invented case files told by shaky narrators, spot claims that clash with reliable records, rebuild timelines from timestamps, and audit which statements the evidence settles.
note: Every narrator, venue, film and record here is invented for this quiz. Each file supplies all the evidence you need, and each has one defensible answer.

sections.title: Cracked Claims
sections.description: Find the claim the reliable record contradicts.

sections.title: Timestamp Timelines
sections.description: Order events using only the clues given.

sections.title: Verdict Audit
sections.description: Judge what the evidence settles.

questions.prompt: Ines narrates her night at an invented editing studio. Which of her claims conflicts with the reliable log?
questions.context: Reliable door log: Ines entered the studio at 7:40 pm and exited at 9:10 pm.

options.label: I left before half past nine.
I was in the studio at 8:30.

questions.explanation: The log shows an exit at 9:10 pm, so staying inside until ten is impossible. The other claims all fit a 7:40 to 9:10 stay.

questions.prompt: Tomas, an invented projectionist, tells his story. Which claim cannot be true given the badge record?
questions.context: Reliable badge record: Tomas badged out of the booth at 6:20 pm and did not badge in again until 8:20 pm. The film started at 6:30 pm and ended at 8:10 pm.

options.label: I started the film from the booth at 6:30.
I was in the booth at 6:10.
I came back to the booth after the film ended.
I left the booth before the film began.

questions.explanation: Tomas was out of the booth from 6:20 to 8:20, so he could not start a 6:30 film from there. The other claims fit the badge times.

questions.prompt: A narrator describes opening night at a small invented hall. Which claim breaks the box-office numbers?
questions.context: Reliable records: the hall has 50 seats. The box office sold 38 tickets and issued 9 complimentary tickets. All 47 ticket holders were scanned in. Nobody else entered.

options.label: Forty-seven people came through the door.

questions.explanation: 38 plus 9 gives 47 attendees, not 50. That leaves 3 empty seats, so claiming a full 50 conflicts with the records.

questions.prompt: Dara, an invented stage actor, recalls a costume change. Which claim does the continuous camera clip contradict?
questions.context: Reliable wardrobe camera: one unbroken clip from 6:00 to 6:10 pm shows the red coat hanging untouched on its hook the whole time.

options.label: I wore the red coat during my 6:03 entrance.
I put the coat on after 6:10.
I last touched the coat before six.

questions.explanation: The coat never left its hook between 6:00 and 6:10, so it could not be worn at 6:03. The other claims fall outside that window.

questions.prompt: Order these four records from earliest to latest, taking care with the pm and am labels.
questions.context: An invented narrator's night is reconstructed from four reliable timestamped records, shown here in no useful order.
questions.explanation: 11:20 pm comes before 11:50 pm, and both come before midnight. After midnight, 12:05 am precedes 12:40 am.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four events so every reliable clue holds. Any order that satisfies the clues is accepted.
questions.context: Reliable clues: the vault card swipe happened after both the call ending and the lift entry. The siren sounded after the vault card swipe. No clue orders the call ending against the lift entry.
questions.explanation: The swipe must follow both earlier events and precede the siren. The call and lift entry can swap places because no clue ranks them.

questions.prompt: Match each of Nell's statements to what the reliable evidence says about it.
questions.context: Reliable evidence: Nell's bus pass tapped on at 5:10 pm. The invented Pier Gallery was open 5:00 to 7:00 pm and screened a film at 6:00 pm. No record shows whether Nell entered the gallery.
questions.explanation: The tap supports the bus claim and the hours support the opening time. Closed at 5:30 is contradicted. Nothing shows whether Nell saw the film.

questions.prompt: Judge each narrator's statement about the invented Elm Cinema late show against the ledger.
questions.context: Reliable ledger: the late show at Elm Cinema started at 9:30 pm and ran exactly 90 minutes, ending at 11:00 pm. Nothing records who arrived or when.

cells.label: Aziz: I left at 10:15 after watching the entire film.
Bea: I took my seat at 9:20 before it started.
Chen: The film began after nine o'clock.
Dalia: The film ended before 10:45.

questions.explanation: Aziz and Dalia clash with the 11:00 pm end. Chen fits the 9:30 start. Bea's arrival time appears in no record, so it stays open.

questions.prompt: Arrange these story events into a possible in-story order, earliest first.
questions.context: In the invented film The Salt Lantern, Mara must find the lamp broken before she orders glass or hires Ines. The new glass and Ines's frame must both be ready before the relighting.

items.label: Ines is hired to build the frame

questions.explanation: The discovery comes first and the relighting comes last. Ordering glass and hiring Ines are independent, so either can come second.

questions.prompt: The film opens on the relit lamp, then cuts back to the broken lamp. Which craft step controls that screen order?

options.label: Editing, which arranges shots and scenes

questions.explanation: Editing arranges shots and scenes, so screen order can differ from story order. Tracking, close-ups and zooms describe camera choices, not sequencing.

questions.prompt: Which scene is third on screen but happens first in story time?
questions.context: Screen order in the invented film, with story day: 1) Festival toast, Day 9. 2) Glass ordered, Day 2. 3) Lamp found broken, Day 1. 4) Glass arrives, Day 6.

title: Read the Rating Label
description: Practice reading screen-rating labels using two invented rating boards with supplied rules: separate age categories from content advisories, decode advisory wording, and spot what a label cannot tell you.

questions.prompt: Connect each board's age label to the category definition that board publishes.

right.label: Admission limited to ages 18 and up

questions.prompt: Sort each Northvale label part as an age category or a content advisory.

cells.label: Open
Mild Fear
Adult 18
Substance Use

questions.explanation: Age categories classify the audience a board recommends or admits. Advisories name kinds of content stated to appear in the film.

questions.prompt: Match each advisory wording to the content meaning its board states.
questions.context: Invented glossary. Northvale Fright: scenes intended to scare. Lakemont Peril: characters are threatened, and harm need not be shown. Northvale Violence: physical harm is shown onscreen. Lakemont Impact: physical harm is shown onscreen.

Characters are threatened in the film

options.label: Both are recommended for ages 14 and up
Both contain the same amount of violence
Both run for the same length

questions.prompt: For a Northvale Open label with no advisories, mark each statement as supported or not supported.

The film suits every child's taste.

questions.explanation: A label reports a classification and listed advisories. Genre and personal taste are outside what the board states.

R16 means more violence than Teen 14

title: Sound Design Ear Test
description: Play short original tone cues, decode them with a supplied sound key, match cues to sources, order a mix checklist, and answer two film-fact questions.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Using the key, which everyday sound is it standing in for?
questions.context: Invented sound key: slow low pulses mean footsteps; fast high pulses mean a clock ticking; one held mid-pitch tone means a fridge hum.
questions.transcript: Five very short 900 Hz sine pulses, evenly spaced a quarter of a second apart.
questions.explanation: The cue is fast and high-pitched, which the key assigns to a clock tick. Footsteps would be slow and low, and a hum would be one held tone.

questions.prompt: Match each cue description to the sound source it represents on the cue sheet.
questions.context: Invented cue sheet: evenly spaced low pulses mean walking; one long high tone means a kettle whistle; a quick pair of mid taps means a knock at a door.
questions.explanation: Each description lines up with one rule on the sheet: low even pulses are walking, the long high tone is the whistle, and the quick pair is the knock. Rain has no cue.

questions.prompt: Count only the phone rings. How many rings does this cue contain?
questions.context: Invented key: one ring is a close pair of 600 Hz pulses. A single low 300 Hz thud is a door knock, not a ring.
questions.transcript: Two close pairs of 600 Hz pulses, separated by a pause, followed by one low 300 Hz thud.
questions.explanation: Each ring is a pair of pulses, so four pulses make two rings. The final low thud is the knock and is excluded.

questions.prompt: Arrange the invented studio's footstep-sound checklist so every stated rule is respected.
questions.context: Rules: recording comes before labeling files and before choosing the best take. Labeling and choosing must both happen before syncing to picture. Exporting the mix comes last, after syncing.
questions.explanation: Recording must come first and exporting last, with syncing just before export. Labeling and choosing can happen in either order because no rule ranks them against each other.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. According to the brief, what effect is this pitch pattern designed to create?
questions.context: Invented brief: stepwise climbing pitch builds tension; stepwise falling pitch releases it; one flat repeated pitch signals routine.
questions.transcript: Four triangle-wave tones at 300, 400, 500 and 650 Hz, each 0.4 seconds after the last, climbing in steps.
questions.explanation: The pitch climbs in steps, which the brief defines as building tension. A falling pattern would release it, and a flat repeated pitch would signal routine.

questions.prompt: Using the brief, choose the intended effect for each cue.
questions.context: Invented brief: stepwise falling pitch means settling calm; fast repeated high pulses mean urgency; one long low tone means looming weight. Nothing in the brief calls for comedy.

cells.label: Slow falling steps
Fast repeated high pulses
One long low tone

questions.explanation: Each cue maps to the brief's stated intent: falling steps settle, fast high pulses press, and a long low tone feels heavy. These are the brief's rules, not universal truths.

title: Fan Theory Evidence Board

sections.description: Four boards, each with four clues to classify.

sections.title: Strongest clue
sections.description: Two boards where you rank clues by impact.

questions.prompt: Sort each clue by how it affects the theory that the butler planted the key.
questions.context: Invented show: The Lantern Pier Mysteries. Theory: butler Odile Marsh planted the brass key in the study desk. Established: Odile first entered the manor at 9:00 pm, and the key could only be planted by placing it in that desk.

cells.label: A photo shows the key already in the desk at 8:30 pm.
Odile's glove fingertips carry varnish from that desk.
The study desk is made of oak.
The door log shows Odile alone in the study at 9:20 pm; the key was found at 9:30 pm.

questions.explanation: A key already in place before the butler arrived rules out planting. Touching the desk and being alone there just before discovery fit the theory. Wood type says nothing.

questions.prompt: Sort each clue by its effect on the theory that a timer caused the blackout.
questions.context: Invented show: Beacon Hollow. Theory: a preset timer, not a person, cut the lighthouse power at exactly 11:40 pm. Established: the switch panel can be set by timer or by hand.

cells.label: The panel dial was found set to 11:40.
A guard saw someone pull the panel lever by hand at 11:40.
The lighthouse tower was painted white last spring.
An intact tape seal covered the panel door from 10:00 pm to 11:50 pm.

questions.explanation: A matching dial and an untouched seal make a manual cause less likely. An eyewitness to a hand pull directly contradicts the timer. The paint colour is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Sort each clue by its effect on the theory that Nora attended the gala as Ines.
questions.context: Invented show: Velvet Tide. Theory: twin sister Nora attended the gala pretending to be Ines. Established: the twins look alike and exactly one of them was at the gala.

cells.label: A gala photo shows a scar on the guest's left wrist; Nora has that scar, Ines does not.
The guest's coat-check ticket was green.
A ferry scan places Nora on a ferry far from the gala all evening.
Ines's passport shows she left the country the day before and returned after the gala.

questions.explanation: Since only one twin attended, evidence placing Ines abroad or matching Nora's scar supports the theory. Nora being elsewhere weakens it. A ticket colour distinguishes neither twin.

questions.prompt: Sort each clue by its effect on the theory that detective Wen Ro sent the 3:15 pm leak.
questions.context: Invented show: Night Desk. Theory: Wen Ro sent the 3:15 pm leak. Established: the leak came from a records terminal that requires someone to log in in person.

cells.label: The leaked file's name uses the shorthand Wen uses in every case file.
Wen drives a blue car.
Camera footage shows Wen in an interrogation room, without a phone, from 3:00 to 3:30 pm.
Only Wen and the captain hold logins for that terminal, and the captain was on leave.

questions.explanation: The shorthand and the shortlist of login holders point toward Wen. Being on camera elsewhere during an in-person login points away. Car colour is unrelated.

questions.prompt: Which clue gives the strongest support for the night manager theory?
questions.context: Invented show: Harbor Inn. Theory: night manager Pell produced the attic creak using a rope-and-pulley rig. Choose the clue that most strongly supports this theory.

options.label: Pell's keycard opened the attic door on two of the six creak nights.
A rope-and-pulley rig stamped with Pell's name hung from the attic beam, matching fresh scuffs on it.
On the loudest creak night, Pell was on a live lobby video call for the full hour; the rig needs a person in the attic.
The attic floorboards are old pine.

questions.explanation: A rig bearing Pell's name that matches the beam damage links Pell directly to the mechanism. The keycard hits are partial, the call weakens the theory, and the pine floor is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Which clue most strongly weakens the night manager theory?
questions.context: Same theory: Pell made the attic creak with a rope-and-pulley rig. Choose the clue that most strongly weakens it.

options.label: Pell's keycard opened the attic door on two of the six creak nights.
A rope-and-pulley rig stamped with Pell's name hung from the attic beam, matching fresh scuffs on it.
On the loudest creak night, Pell was on a live lobby video call for the full hour; the rig needs a person in the attic.
The attic floorboards are old pine.

questions.explanation: If the rig needs someone in the attic and Pell was demonstrably in the lobby, Pell could not have made the loudest creak. The other clues support or do nothing.

questions.prompt: Which clue gives the strongest support for the projectionist theory?
questions.context: Invented show: Reel Hours. Theory: projectionist Dara took the missing reel between 8:00 and 9:00 pm on Friday.

options.label: The reel was on its vault shelf at 8:00 pm and the shelf was empty at 9:00 pm.
Dara's badge opened the vault at 8:41 pm.
Dara was one of four staff members holding a vault key.
The loading-door alarm sounded at 8:15 pm, and Dara's badge first entered the building at 8:30 pm.

questions.explanation: A badge opening the vault inside the window ties Dara to the right place and time. The window alone names no one, a key is shared by four, and the alarm points away.

questions.prompt: Which clue most strongly weakens the projectionist theory?
questions.context: Same theory: Dara took the reel between 8:00 and 9:00 pm on Friday. Choose the clue that most strongly weakens it.

options.label: The reel was on its vault shelf at 8:00 pm and the shelf was empty at 9:00 pm.
Dara's badge opened the vault at 8:41 pm.
Dara was one of four staff members holding a vault key.
The loading-door alarm sounded at 8:15 pm, and Dara's badge first entered the building at 8:30 pm.

questions.explanation: An alarm before Dara even entered suggests the reel may have left earlier through another route. The other clues either fit the theory or merely set the time window.

She has been demoted at work

She has forgotten her old coat

The jacket now belongs to someone else
She is hiding from a crowd

She has bought a more expensive coat

options.label: They are starting to find common ground
They have forgotten who is who
They are leaving the family business

questions.context: Invented film note: a designer lists four intended set effects: rising pressure, time frozen by a past event, being cut off from outside, and growing isolation. Match each set choice to the effect it was built for.

A window blocked by stacked boxes
A clock stopped at 4:10 in every room
One table with fewer chairs each act

Brief: show a very tidy character losing control

Labels peeling and stacks spilling over

title: Showrunner's Season Planner

Repeat the pilot's reliable format for several episodes

questions.explanation: Rooms solve slumps in different ways. Your pick hints at whether you protect structure or let the story wander.

Let a character-focused episode break the usual formula

Deliver a twist that reframes earlier episodes

title: Three Ways to Follow the Dialogue
description: Eight tasks on screen-access features: choose the feature that meets a stated viewing need, then match original example lines and menu labels to captions, subtitles, dubbing or audio description.

sections.description: Each viewer states a need.

sections.title: Match the examples
sections.description: Connect invented lines and labels to features.

questions.prompt: Ines wants written dialogue plus sound cues, all in the same language as the audio. Which feature gives her both?
questions.context: Working definitions for this quiz: captions = same-language text with speaker names and sound cues; subtitles = translated dialogue text; dubbing = replacement voices in another language; audio description = narrated visuals.
questions.explanation: Captions pair same-language dialogue with cues such as music or doors. Subtitles translate, dubbing replaces voices, and audio description narrates what is seen.

questions.prompt: Tomas is blind and loses track of silent action, like a character crossing a room. Which feature addresses that need?
questions.context: Working definitions: captions = same-language text with sound cues; subtitles = translated text; dubbing = replacement voices; audio description = narration of visual action in gaps.
questions.explanation: Audio description narrates visual action during pauses. The other three deal with dialogue language or text, not with what appears on screen.

questions.prompt: Wen is watching a film recorded in a language she doesn't speak. She wants to hear voices she understands, without reading. Which feature fits?
questions.context: Working definitions: captions = same-language text with sound cues; subtitles = translated text; dubbing = replacement voices in another language; audio description = narration of visuals.
questions.explanation: Dubbing swaps the spoken track for voices in her language, so no reading is needed. Subtitles and captions both require reading text.

questions.prompt: Dara hears fine and wants the original voices of a film in a language she doesn't speak, plus translated lines to read. What fits?
questions.context: Working definitions: captions = same-language text with sound cues; subtitles = translated text over original voices; dubbing = replacement voices; audio description = narration of visuals.
questions.explanation: Subtitles keep the original performances and add translated text. Dubbing would remove the original voices, and captions stay in the audio's own language.

questions.prompt: Match each invented example to the access feature it shows.
questions.context: Invented scenes from a fictional film. Working definitions: captions = same-language text with cues; subtitles = translated text; dubbing = replaced voices; audio description = narrated visuals.

questions.explanation: The thunder cue and speaker name mark captions. Translated text over original audio is subtitles, swapped voices are dubbing, and narrated action is audio description.

questions.prompt: Match each viewer need to the feature that meets it. Some features can be used more than once.

A hearing viewer wants English text over Italian voices
A viewer wants speaker names and [phone buzzes] shown on screen

title: How Scares Work
description: Identify four original non-graphic scenes by scare mechanic, match each technique to its effect, order the beats of a tense scene, and answer two film-craft questions.

questions.prompt: A slow camera creeps down an empty hallway while a clock ticks and nothing happens yet. Which mechanic is this?
questions.context: Quiz glossary: Dread is tension from expecting something that has not happened. A jump scare is a sudden loud or fast event after quiet. Uncanny means familiar but subtly wrong. A false alarm is a threat revealed as harmless.
questions.explanation: Nothing has happened, and the fear comes from waiting and anticipating. That slow-building expectation is dread.

questions.prompt: A lifelike doll at a dinner table smiles and turns its head smoothly, but its eyes sit slightly too far apart. Which mechanic?
questions.context: Glossary: Dread is expecting something that has not happened. Jump scare is a sudden event after quiet. Uncanny means familiar but subtly wrong. False alarm is a threat revealed as harmless.
questions.explanation: The doll is almost human but slightly off, which creates the unease of the uncanny. Nothing is being awaited and nothing startles.

questions.prompt: A character hears scratching, opens the cupboard, and finds a wind-up toy tapping the wall. She laughs and relaxes. Which mechanic?
questions.context: Glossary: Dread is expecting something that has not happened. Jump scare is a sudden event after quiet. Uncanny means familiar but subtly wrong. False alarm is a threat revealed as harmless.
questions.explanation: The apparent threat turns out to be harmless, releasing tension. Filmmakers often use this to lower the audience's guard before a real scare.

questions.prompt: In a silent reading nook, a window slams with a loud bang and a shape bursts into frame within half a second. Which mechanic?
questions.context: Glossary: Dread is expecting something that has not happened. Jump scare is a sudden loud or fast event after quiet. Uncanny means familiar but subtly wrong. False alarm is a threat revealed as harmless.
questions.explanation: A sudden loud, fast event after quiet is a jump scare. The viewer has almost no time to anticipate it.

questions.prompt: Match each scare mechanic to the effect it mainly creates on the audience.

right.label: Unease at something almost normal but wrong

questions.explanation: Dread builds tension through waiting, jump scares startle, the uncanny unsettles through near-normal wrongness, and false alarms give relief.

questions.prompt: Order the beats of a tense scene so each beat sets up the next one.
questions.context: Invented scene: a woman returns to a quiet apartment. The beats are shuffled; each must follow the one it depends on.

items.label: Reveal what is behind the door
Hold a long quiet shot on the shut door
Notice a small wrong detail, a door ajar

questions.explanation: Establishing normality makes the wrong detail stand out. Holding the quiet shot then stretches the tension before the reveal pays it off.

questions.prompt: A director wants viewers to stare at a doorknob slowly turning. Which shot isolates that small detail?

options.label: Wide establishing shot of the house
Over-the-shoulder shot of two people talking

questions.explanation: An extreme close-up isolates a small detail, filling the frame with it. That makes a tiny movement feel important.

questions.prompt: An editor lets silence run under a still hallway shot, then cuts to a monster with a loud hit. What did editing do?

options.label: Changed the camera lens during the shot
Removed the need for any image
Turned the monster into a different character
Combined image and sound timing to create a startle

questions.explanation: Editing arranges shots and combines image with sound. Placing a loud sound exactly on the cut creates the sudden startle.

title: Documentary, Docudrama, or Mockumentary?

sections.description: Spot cues and craft steps.

questions.prompt: Which form fits this invented film?
questions.context: Working definitions here: a documentary presents real people and events as fact; a docudrama has actors dramatize events presented as true; a mockumentary uses documentary style for an invented story, usually comedic. Film: actors play bakery staff in a made-up comedy, speaking to camera in interviews, with shaky handheld shots.

options.label: Straight drama with no documentary styling

questions.explanation: Interviews to camera and handheld shots borrow documentary style, while the actors and invented story make it fake nonfiction played for comedy.

questions.prompt: Which form fits the film about the harbour strike?
questions.context: Film: inside this puzzle's invented world, a harbour strike really happened. The film uses actors performing scripted scenes of the negotiations, with dialogue built from the union's meeting minutes.
questions.explanation: Actors recreate events the film presents as true, with scripted dialogue. That dramatization of a real event is the docudrama signature.

questions.prompt: Match each invented film description to its form.

left.label: Archive footage and interviews with surviving harbour workers, tied together by a narrator
Actors as lighthouse keepers giving deadpan interviews that parody nature films
Actors reenact a true negotiation, with invented composite dialogue
A camera quietly follows a real choir through a year of rehearsals, with no actors

questions.explanation: Real people and recorded events make documentaries. Actors dramatizing a true event make a docudrama. Actors parodying documentary style in an invented story make a mockumentary.

questions.prompt: What most separates a docudrama from a mockumentary?

options.label: A docudrama always uses handheld cameras
A docudrama dramatizes events presented as true; a mockumentary imitates documentary style for an invented story

questions.explanation: The difference lies in the claim about events, not the camera. Docudramas stage events presented as true, while mockumentaries borrow documentary manner for fiction.

questions.prompt: Match each film-language cue to what it does.
questions.context: A film crew's notes list four cues used in documentary-style films. Pick the effect of each.

cells.label: Extreme close-up of a trembling hand
Tracking shot beside a walking subject
Lens zoom toward a distant sign
Editing interview audio over street images

questions.explanation: An extreme close-up isolates detail. Tracking changes camera position, but a zoom need not. Editing arranges shots and combines image with sound.

questions.prompt: An invented opening card reads: 'Based on a true event; some conversations are imagined.' Which form does it signal?
questions.explanation: The card claims a true basis while admitting imagined dialogue. That blend of real events and dramatization marks a docudrama.

questions.prompt: Which feature signals a mockumentary rather than a documentary?

options.label: Interviewees are credited as actors playing invented people
An extreme close-up isolates a detail

questions.explanation: Handheld shots, narration and close-ups appear in real documentaries too. Invented people performed by actors inside documentary styling is the telltale sign.

questions.prompt: Order this invented studio's documentary workflow. Any order that respects the rules is accepted.
questions.context: Rules: footage must exist before shots are chosen; shots are chosen before they are arranged; narration is written to fit the arranged scene, so it comes last.

items.label: Arrange chosen shots into a scene
Lay narration over the arranged scene

questions.explanation: Editing arranges selected shots, so recording and selecting come first. Under this studio's rule, narration is fitted to the arranged scene afterward.

title: Story Shapes: Telenovela to Anthology
description: Match five TV series formats to their storytelling promise, reason through a format-trait map and a release schedule, then name the format behind four original series pitches.

sections.title: Format promises
sections.description: What each shape of series offers viewers

sections.title: Pitch check
sections.description: Name the format behind four invented pitches

questions.prompt: Match each series format to the storytelling promise it makes to viewers.
questions.explanation: Each format is defined by how it handles endings, casts and plot threads. Procedurals reset weekly, anthologies reset entirely, limited series end quickly, open-ended serials keep going, and telenovela-style serials build to a planned finale.

right.label: A fresh case or problem each episode, with a returning core team
A new story, and often a new cast, each installment
One complete story told in a handful of episodes, any genre
Plot threads continue season after season with no planned end
Romance and family melodrama with escalating secrets, serialized toward a planned finale

questions.prompt: A viewer joins midway through a run and wants each episode to make sense alone. Which format promise suits them best?
questions.explanation: A procedural closes its main case inside each episode, so a newcomer can follow without earlier plot. Serial formats rely on threads built over many episodes.

options.label: Procedural: a new case closes each episode
Open-ended serial: threads build across seasons
Telenovela-style serial: secrets escalate toward a finale
Limited series: one story unfolds in order

questions.prompt: Link each format to every trait it promises. Some formats share a trait.
questions.explanation: Anthologies may change cast and setting; procedurals bring a core team to a new case; serials and telenovela-style shows carry threads forward; only the telenovela-style show builds toward a planned finale.
questions.context: Working definitions: an anthology tells a separate story each installment; a procedural closes a new case each episode with a returning team; an open-ended serial carries threads onward with no set end; a telenovela-style serial carries threads toward a planned finale.

right.label: Cast and setting may change between installments
Core team returns to handle a new case each episode
Unresolved plot threads carry into the next episode
Story is built toward a planned finale

questions.prompt: In which week does the finale of this invented limited series air?
questions.explanation: Episodes 1–6 air in weeks 1–3, week 4 is the break, episodes 7–8 air in week 5, and the last two episodes, 9 and 10, air in week 6.
questions.context: Invented schedule: the limited series 'Lantern Row' has 10 episodes. Two air each week starting in week 1, with no airings in week 4, then two per week resume in week 5.

questions.prompt: Which format does this invented pitch describe?
questions.explanation: A new cast and an unrelated mystery each season mean no story carries over, which is the anthology promise. A procedural would keep a returning core team.
questions.context: Pitch: 'Harbor Lights' visits a different island town each season, with a new cast and a mystery unrelated to earlier seasons.

questions.prompt: Which format fits the pitch for 'The Quiet Ledger'?
questions.explanation: The same three colleagues return and every case ends by the credits. That is a procedural, not an anthology, because the core team persists.
questions.context: Pitch: in 'The Quiet Ledger', the same forensic accountant and two colleagues untangle a new fraud case every episode. Each case closes before the credits.

questions.prompt: Which format fits the pitch for 'Salt and Silk'?
questions.explanation: Rival families, hidden parentage and weekly melodrama pointing to a set finale fit a telenovela-style serial. At 120 episodes it is not the handful of episodes a limited series implies.
questions.context: Pitch: 'Salt and Silk' follows two rival families, a hidden parentage secret and a wedding interrupted again and again. The writers announce the story ends at episode 120.

questions.prompt: Which format fits the pitch for 'Orbit Station'?
questions.explanation: Open threads, no announced end and yearly renewal describe an open-ended serial. It is not a limited series, since no finale is planned.
questions.context: Pitch: 'Orbit Station' follows one crew across years. Each episode leaves threads open, no end date is announced, and the show is renewed year by year.

title: Poster Grammar Lab
description: Decode the layout, framing, color and text conventions of movie posters using original schematic mock-ups, then rank elements by visual weight and stack them in layers.

questions.prompt: Using the lab rule below, which zone of this mock-up works as the poster's focal point?
questions.context: Lab rule: a focal point is the element with the largest area and the strongest contrast against its background. The diagram is an original schematic with no real poster.

diagram.title: Mock-up A: four text and mark zones
diagram.description: A tall schematic poster. From top to bottom: a small pale tagline, a wide dim cast strip, a very large bright title block, and a small bright studio mark at lower left.

zones.label: Small pale tagline at the top edge
Small bright studio mark at lower left

options.label: Small pale tagline at the top edge
Small bright studio mark at lower left

questions.explanation: The title block is both the biggest area and the highest-contrast element, so it wins. The bright studio mark has contrast but is far too small to dominate.

questions.prompt: A mock poster shows a tiny figure beneath a huge dark sky. What effect does that scale contrast usually create?

options.label: Isolation and the vastness surrounding the figure
The feel of a crowded ensemble cast
Close, intimate emotional contact with the figure

questions.explanation: A small subject inside a large empty field makes the surroundings feel enormous and the figure alone. Crowds and intimacy come from many faces or tight framing instead.

questions.prompt: A mock poster crops so a single eye fills the whole frame. Which film term names this framing?
questions.explanation: An extreme close-up isolates a small detail, such as an eye. Tracking involves moving the camera position, and a zoom changes the lens, not the framing of one detail.

questions.prompt: A leading line is an element whose direction pulls the eye toward the subject. Which zone is the leading line?

diagram.title: Mock-up B: lone figure at the horizon
diagram.description: A schematic poster. A dark sky block fills the top. Below it a small lit figure stands at the horizon. A pale road wedge narrows from the bottom toward the figure. A title strip runs along the bottom edge.

zones.label: Dark empty sky block across the top
Pale road wedge narrowing toward the horizon figure
Small lit figure at the horizon
Title strip along the bottom edge

options.label: Dark empty sky block across the top
Pale road wedge narrowing toward the horizon figure
Small lit figure at the horizon
Title strip along the bottom edge

questions.explanation: The road narrows toward the figure, so its converging edges guide the eye there. The figure is the destination, the sky is empty space, and the title strip is text.

questions.prompt: Pick the genre each mock-up's design most conventionally signals.
questions.context: Poster conventions are tendencies, not rules. Each cell describes one original mock-up.

cells.label: Pastel palette, two people facing each other at center, rounded script title
Black and red palette, a half-lit face off center, cramped jagged capitals
Cool blue-silver palette, glowing grid lines, a ringed planet, wide-spaced metallic capitals
Saturated primary colors, bubbly rounded lettering, cartoon animals bunched in a bouncy group

questions.explanation: Soft color with paired figures reads romantic, harsh contrast reads menacing, cold tech motifs read sci-fi, and bright rounded cartoons read family animation. These are conventions that real posters sometimes break.

questions.prompt: Match each poster element to the job it usually does.

right.label: Sets the mood before any word is read
Names the film in distinctive type
Lists credits in tiny condensed type

questions.explanation: Taglines hook in one line, billing blocks pack in credits, title lettering gives the film a typographic identity, and color delivers mood instantly.

questions.prompt: Order these poster text elements from most to least visually prominent.
questions.context: Lab rule: larger type with strong contrast ranks higher. All text is white or gray on black. Tagline: 18 pt light gray. Billing block: 7 pt mid gray. Title: 120 pt white. Cast names: 36 pt white.
questions.explanation: Title at 120 pt leads, cast names at 36 pt follow, then the 18 pt gray tagline, and the tiny 7 pt billing block ends up least prominent.

questions.prompt: Put these mock-up layers in a valid drawing order, back layer first.
questions.context: Overlap facts: the figure stands in front of the sky. The title text sits in front of the figure's legs. The small billing text sits over the lower sky only and touches nothing else.
questions.explanation: Whatever overlaps something must be drawn after it: sky, then figure, then title. Billing text only needs the sky behind it, so it can go anywhere after the sky.

note: All posters are original schematic mock-ups described in text and diagrams, not real posters, logos or stills. Genre signals are design conventions, and real posters often break them.

title: Foley Booth Phantom Mix
description: Calibrate recorded Foley cues for a phantom film sequence using an invented 24 fps studio frame clock. Distinguish too-early or too-late offsets, compute latency adjustments, and identify simultaneously aligned cues. All rules and the frame clock are explicit original fiction for this toy model.

questions.prompt: A Foley cue is marked +3 frames (late) relative to the visual hit on the invented 24 fps clock. What time delay in milliseconds must be subtracted to align it?
questions.context: Invented studio rule: frame rate is exactly 24 fps. Time per frame = 1000/24 ms. Positive frames mean the audio starts after the visual (late). Subtract the equivalent time to correct late cues. Negative means early (add time).
questions.explanation: 3 / 24 * 1000 = 125 ms exactly. Subtract 125 ms to correct the late cue.

questions.prompt: Order the correction steps for a +2 frame late Foley footstep cue.
questions.context: Invented procedure: Measure frame offset, convert frames to ms (frames * 1000/24), subtract the ms from audio start, verify simultaneous alignment with visual.

items.label: Subtract the ms from audio start

questions.explanation: Measure first, convert, subtract to correct late, then verify.

questions.prompt: Match each frame offset to its meaning on the invented clock.
questions.context: Positive offset = audio late. Negative = audio early. Zero = aligned.
questions.explanation: Sign indicates direction of offset relative to visual.

questions.prompt: Select the correct latency direction for each cue.
questions.context: Late positive → subtract; early negative → add; zero → none. Use 1000/24 ≈41.67 ms/frame.

cells.label: +5 frames
-3 frames
0 frames

questions.explanation: +5 subtract ~208 ms; -3 add ~125 ms; zero no change.

questions.prompt: Connect every cue to its status after the listed latency adjustment. Connect ALL valid links by the rule; false positives penalized.
questions.context: Visual at t=0. Adjustments: CueA +166.7ms adjust -166.7ms (aligns); CueB +83.3ms adjust -50ms (remains late); CueC -41.7ms adjust +41.7ms (aligns); CueD +125ms adjust -100ms (remains late).
questions.explanation: CueA and CueC exact cancel so align. CueB and CueD partial cancel so remain late. All valid links shown; no arbitrary pairs.

questions.prompt: Symbolic tones: visual flash (high) and Foley hit (low). Using text alternative, is the Foley early, late, or aligned?
questions.context: Flash delay 0.500 s, Foley 0.542 s. 1 frame ≈ 41.7 ms. Aligned if |diff| ≤ 20.8 ms.
questions.transcript: Symbolic tones: high-frequency tone (visual flash role) starts at delay 0.500 seconds, duration 0.1 s; low-frequency tone (Foley hit role) starts at delay 0.542 seconds, duration 0.1 s.
questions.explanation: Difference of 42 ms is approximately one frame (41.7 ms) late relative to the visual flash. Outside zero-tolerance alignment.

questions.prompt: A phantom whisper is -2 frames early. What latency adjustment is required?
questions.context: Early (negative) requires adding the positive equivalent time. 2 frames = 2*(1000/24) ms.
questions.explanation: Add 83.3 ms to delay the early cue into alignment.

questions.prompt: Match each adjusted start to simultaneous status with visual at t=0.
questions.context: Simultaneous only if residual start time is exactly 0 after adjustment.
questions.explanation: Exact cancel (l1, l3, l4) simultaneous; residual positive (l2) still late. Reused target for simultaneous is allowed.

sources.label: Original fictional Foley booth phantom mix with invented 24 fps frame clock

note: All scenarios original fiction/synthetic. Invented frame clock. Audio symbolic with exact text alternative. No real production advice. Graphs list every valid link; matches reuse targets only when semantically identical by rule.

title: The Glasshouse Cut: Who Looks Guilty?
description: Restore missing shots and displaced sound in an original haunted trailer. A caretaker looks guilty, a rescue emerges, and one final image refuses to be explained.

questions.prompt: What accusation does this cut invite that the two shots do not establish?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. The Glasshouse After Closing: a volunteer, Imani, and caretaker Ellis are packing a closed conservatory. Trailer shot A: Ellis looks toward a glass door. Shot B: Imani recoils as a tall shadow crosses frosted glass. There is no shared view showing what Ellis sees or where he stands relative to Imani.
questions.explanation: A followed by B invites a connection between Ellis and the shadow, but the cut supplies no view connecting them in space. Imani’s reaction and Ellis’s look are visible; the accusation is an inference the trailer encourages.

options.label: Ellis is the figure frightening Imani.
Imani notices a shadow on the glass.
The trailer shows two people in separate shots.

questions.prompt: Which detail in the restored wide shot most directly changes the meaning of Ellis’s hand?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. A close crop shows Ellis’s hand pressed against the door edge, with the handle and lower doorway out of view. Cut against Imani pulling, it makes him look like an obstacle. In the restored wide shot a fallen metal plant stand lies across the door’s bottom edge. Imani pulls from inside while Ellis pushes from outside.
questions.explanation: The stand explains the obstruction, and the wide shot shows both people trying to open the door. The crop suggested that Ellis held it shut; the restored action instead makes him a helper.

options.label: The door is made of glass.
The plant stand prevents the door from swinging.

questions.prompt: Which recovered shot would establish a physical source for the silhouette, rather than just another coincidence?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. A roof vent rattles and a moving silhouette crosses the frosted door as Imani recoils. The intervening shot is missing. The continuity report places the following candidate inserts at that same moment; it does not identify the silhouette’s source. Which insert actually connects an object, the light and the image on the glass?
questions.explanation: Only the continuous view supplies the whole projection path and ties its movement together. A coat moving somewhere nearby is a possible lead, but coincidence in time does not locate it between this lamp and this glass. The other inserts show reactions or a different doorway.

options.label: A coat sways in a close-up, but neither the lamp nor the glass is visible.
Ellis reaches toward a different door in the corridor.
One continuous view shows the coat between lamp and glass, its swinging edge tracing the silhouette’s movement.
Imani turns her head in the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Restore these three sounds to the footage where they were recorded.
questions.context: Original fictional scene. Sound report: GREENHOUSE TAKE has a loose latch rattling at the jammed door. PACKING TAKE has Imani say “Don’t leave it here” while pointing to an unlabelled parcel. STREET TAKE has a bicycle brake squeal as a cyclist stops outside. The trailer moved all three under Ellis approaching the glass.
questions.explanation: The rattle belongs to the door, the line concerns a parcel, and the squeal comes from the street. Moving them under Ellis assembles a threatening encounter that none of the original recordings contains.

left.label: “Don’t leave it here” under his approach
The squeal under his raised hand

right.label: The latch at the jammed door

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the four fragments from the changing object states.
questions.context: Original fictional scene. These fragments belong to one continuous event, which starts with the parcel inside and the door shut. Once opened, the door is not shut again. The stand is not put back into an earlier position between fragments, and the parcel is placed outside only once. Use what is upright, fallen, cleared or open in the cards; their list order is scrambled.
questions.explanation: An upright stand being caught by the coat precedes a fallen stand blocking the shut door. Clearing that fallen stand comes next; the open doorway and parcel outside come after the obstruction is removed. The object states force c → b → d → a without a timestamp or a narrated sequence.

items.label: Door open; stand set upright by the wall; Imani puts the parcel outside.
Door shut; the fallen stand crosses its bottom edge; Imani pulls.
Door shut; the stand is upright as the swinging coat catches it.
Door still shut; Ellis lifts the fallen stand clear of its swing.

questions.prompt: Which recorded detail prevents the earlier lamp-and-coat mechanism from explaining the new image?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. A later locked-camera shot shows a hand-shaped patch forming on the glass. The earlier silhouette had been cast by a coat intercepting the work lamp. All four observations below are recorded in this later shot. Which removes an ingredient that the earlier mechanism needed?
questions.explanation: The earlier projection needed light from the work lamp, which is now unpowered. The people’s positions, the glass and the parcel do not by themselves remove that light source. This rules out reusing that specific explanation; it does not establish what made the new mark or prove a ghost.

options.label: Ellis and Imani are both outside.
The mark is on the same glass door.
The work lamp is unplugged and its light is off.
The parcel is resting on the outside bench.

questions.prompt: Which single edit repairs this misleading cut while retaining every shot and every spoken word?
questions.context: Original fictional scene. The revised trailer already shows the jam and rescue honestly. It then shows Imani pointing at the parcel as she says “Don’t leave it here.” The picture cuts to the forming hand mark before she reaches “here,” so her sentence now seems to refer to the mark. All shots and the original line must remain. Choose a repair to the picture–sound relationship, not a new explanation of the mark.
questions.explanation: Holding the pointing shot through the full line keeps its referent visible; the condensation can still follow as the last image. Cutting earlier strengthens the false connection, rewriting the line changes the supplied words, and volume alone does not restore its subject. Suspense remains in the unexplained image rather than a misassigned warning.

options.label: Cut away from the parcel even earlier, leaving more of the line over the mark.
Hold the pointing-at-parcel shot until the line ends, then cut to the mark.
Keep the cut, but replace “here” with “on the glass.”
Keep the cut and lower the line’s volume while it continues over the mark.

questions.prompt: Choose the last line for your version of the trailer.
questions.context: Original fictional scene. Your restored edit shows that the coat made the shadow, the fallen stand jammed the door, and Ellis helped free it. The final condensation remains unexplained. All four captions fit that footage; choose the voice you prefer. This creative choice is ungraded and does not change the story or the earlier answers.
questions.explanation: All four captions preserve the rescue and the unexplained mark. They offer different styles: an image, a question, a contrast or a spare observation. This is your creative finish, so it is shown in review but does not count toward accuracy.

options.label: “The door opens. The glass keeps a secret.”
“Someone helped her out. What stayed behind?”
“The rescue is over. The mystery isn’t.”

title: The Pumpkin Puppet and the Lost Star
description: Read an original pumpkin stop-motion storyboard, choose what each frame makes visible, and turn an apparent threat into an act of help. End by choosing the image you would leave with the audience.

sources.label: Original fictional stop-motion storyboard and prop continuity notes

note: Text storyboards for an original fictional short, not displayed animation or photographs. Seven craft tasks have keyed answers under stated goals; one artistic finish is ungraded. No film-history, validated creativity or personality claim.

questions.prompt: What first tells you the scarecrow has lost something, rather than deliberately put it down?
questions.context: Original storyboard: a paper star is sewn to the scarecrow's chest in frame A. A gust bends the stalk in B; the thread snaps and the star lands in a puddle in C. Its empty stitch remains visible.
questions.explanation: The stitched star has a visible before, break, and after state. Its move is caused by the snapped thread, not an unseen choice.

options.label: The star changes from attached to loose after the thread snaps
The pumpkin appears at the edge of frame C

questions.prompt: Which next frame would show the pumpkin has noticed the star?
questions.context: In C the pumpkin faces away from the puddle. The craft brief asks for one small pose change that makes its attention legible before it rolls anywhere.
questions.explanation: A changed gaze with the body still in place supplies a readable reaction without skipping the discovery.

options.label: Keep its face fixed and move the camera farther back
Turn its carved eyes toward the star while its body stays put
Remove the star from the puddle between frames

questions.prompt: Match each framing decision to the piece of story information it can reveal.
questions.context: Three proposed text storyboard stills crop the same original set differently. Match what remains visible in each crop; do not assume anything outside it is shown.
questions.explanation: Each crop makes different evidence available: the damaged stitch, the geography of the set, or a reaction. Framing chooses what the viewer can notice without adding a new event.

left.label: Only the snapped thread and the empty stitch fill the frame
The full set shows the pumpkin, the puddle and the scarecrow together
The pumpkin’s face fills the frame, with its leaf eyebrow lifting

right.label: The distance and relationship between the characters and fallen prop
The physical trace that connects the missing star to the chest
A change in the pumpkin’s expression

questions.prompt: How can the puppet visibly pick up a wet paper star without a mysterious jump?
questions.context: The pumpkin's vine is beside, but not yet touching, the star. The next still should bridge contact and lifting; no extra hand or unseen helper belongs in this film.
questions.explanation: Contact before lifting makes the transformation from loose prop to carried prop traceable.

options.label: Show the vine curling under one point while the star is still on the puddle
Show the star already on the scarecrow
Cut to a blank screen and narrate the lift

questions.prompt: Arrange three stills so a threatening gesture becomes an act of help.
questions.context: Original craft goal: let the viewer share the pumpkin’s initial worry, then discover why the scarecrow raised its arm, then show the pumpkin accepting the help. The wider view must reveal something the tight reaction view could not show.
questions.explanation: A worried reaction creates the apparent threat; widening reveals the shelter; moving toward it shows the pumpkin has understood. The sequence changes the meaning of an earlier image rather than simply listing prop movements.

items.label: The pumpkin moves back toward the fallen star beneath the new shelter
A tight view shows the pumpkin shrinking from the scarecrow’s raised arm
A wider view reveals the raised arm holding a leaf above the puddle as a shelter

questions.prompt: Why does the pumpkin stop beside a dry leaf before crossing the puddle?
questions.context: Storyboard stills: it puts the wet star on the dry leaf; the leaf's edge absorbs the visible drop. It then lifts the less-drooping star and continues. No dialogue explains the pause.
questions.explanation: The leaf changes the star's visible condition, giving the pause a practical story purpose.

options.label: It is hiding the star from the scarecrow
It is letting the fragile star dry before returning it
It has forgotten where the scarecrow stands

questions.prompt: Which tiny motion communicates each beat without a caption?
questions.context: Original storyboard notes: the scarecrow's stitched arm can tilt; the pumpkin's eyebrow is a separate leaf; the chest star can be reattached. Choose one distinct visible change for each beat.
questions.explanation: The arm answers the helper, the eyebrow changes the pumpkin's expression, and the chest state closes the star's journey.

right.label: Star returns to its chest stitches
Leaf eyebrow relaxes above the pumpkin's eyes
Scarecrow arm tips toward the pumpkin

questions.prompt: Which final still would you choose for this wordless short?
questions.context: The star has been restored and the pumpkin is leaving. Choose what the audience gets to carry away from the same completed action. These are artistic alternatives, not a test of filmmaking taste.
questions.explanation: The stitch emphasizes repair, the distant gesture emphasizes connection, and the empty set emphasizes what remains after a meeting. Each can end the same story; your choice is ungraded.

options.label: Hold on the repaired stitch: a tiny piece of work has made the scarecrow whole again
Hold a wide gap between them while one arm slowly lifts in farewell
Show the empty puddle and leaf shelter after both characters have left the frame
